newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Investigators of Guatemala crash look at engine.
newsitem.headline: Investigators of Guatemala crash look at engine.

text.p: A failed engine may have caused Friday's crash of a small tourist aircraft that killed 14 people but a complete report will not be ready for three months, officials said on Monday.

"Now that we've identified the motors we have a doubt about the second motor, which seems to not have been functioning at full power," Hugo Mayen, chief of flight security for the Civil Aviation Authority, told reporters.
He said the Brazilian-made Bandeirante turboprop plane came down almost vertically as it was descending to the Santa Elena airport, which serves the world-famous Mayan temple site of Tikal.

The plane belonging to local airline Transportes Aereos Profesionales (TAPSA) crashed in cloudy weather about five miles (8 km) from its destination in Peten province near Guatemala's northern border with Mexico.

Just 500 yards (metres) from the site of Friday's crash a Caravelle aircraft belonging to the Aerovias airline crashed on Jan. 18, 1986, killing 88 people including Venezuelan Foreign Affairs Minister Aristides Calvani.

Mayen said tapes of communications with the control tower showed the pilot of Friday's flight did not declare any mechanical failures, but investigators will send the engines to their Canadian maker for testing. He also said technicians from the Brazilian airplane maker would visit Guatemala to help in the investigation.
There were no survivors of the crash. The dead included the pilot, the co-pilot, 10 Guatemalan tourists and two expatriates, an American and a Briton.

Deborah Ann Young, 40, originally of Amarillo, Texas, was living in Antigua, Guatemala, where she was buried. British-born Patricia de Solis was married to a Guatemalan and had lived in this Central American country for more than 20 years. She and her husband owned the Jaguar Inn, one of three hotels inside the national park that protects the Mayan ruins at Tikal.
